claim: Tissue homeostasis requires a balance between progenitor cell proliferation and loss.
source: Tissue homeostasis requires a balance between progenitor cell proliferation and loss.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about tissue homeostasis.

claim: Asymmetric cell divisions were increased in hyperproliferative conditions.
source: Genetic and pharmacologic experiments demonstrate that asymmetric cell divisions were increased in hyperproliferative conditions and decreased under hypoproliferative conditions.
evidence: The abstract states this was demonstrated through genetic and pharmacologic experiments, indicating experimental data support.

claim: Asymmetric cell divisions were decreased under hypoproliferative conditions.
source: Genetic and pharmacologic experiments demonstrate that asymmetric cell divisions were increased in hyperproliferative conditions and decreased under hypoproliferative conditions.
evidence: The abstract states this was demonstrated through genetic and pharmacologic experiments, indicating experimental data support.

claim: Active K-Ras increased the frequency of asymmetric cell divisions.
source: Further, active K-Ras also increased the frequency of asymmetric cell divisions.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract, supported by experimental data.

claim: Disruption of spindle orientation in combination with constitutively active K-Ras resulted in massive tissue overgrowth.
source: Disruption of spindle orientation in combination with constitutively active K-Ras resulted in massive tissue overgrowth.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract, supported by experimental data.

claim: In aged sun-exposed skin, homeostasis and the architecture of the epidermis is maintained despite prevalent clones of cells containing oncogenic mutations.
source: Remarkably, in aged sun-exposed skin, homeostasis and the architecture of the epidermis is maintained despite prevalent clones of cells containing oncogenic mutations (Martincorena et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Martincorena et al., 2015.

claim: Oncogene-induced differentiation is one mechanism of epidermal robustness.
source: Recent work has highlighted oncogene-induced differentiation and active elimination of mutant clones as two mechanisms of epidermal robustness, suggesting there are multiple modes of response to perturbation (Brown et al., 2017; Ying et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2017 and Ying et al., 2018.

claim: Active elimination of mutant clones is one mechanism of epidermal robustness.
source: Recent work has highlighted oncogene-induced differentiation and active elimination of mutant clones as two mechanisms of epidermal robustness, suggesting there are multiple modes of response to perturbation (Brown et al., 2017; Ying et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2017 and Ying et al., 2018.

claim: Embryonic epidermal progenitors can divide parallel to the basement membrane, resulting in two basal daughter cells (symmetric divisions).
source: Embryonic epidermal progenitors can divide parallel to the basement membrane, resulting in two basal daughter cells, which we term symmetric divisions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about embryonic epidermal cell division.

claim: Embryonic epidermal progenitors can divide perpendicular to the basement membrane.
source: These cells can also divide perpendicular to the basement membrane (Lechler and Fuchs, 2005; Poulson and Lechler, 2010; Smart, 1970; Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Perpendicular divisions contribute one daughter cell to the differentiated suprabasal cell layer and do not alter the number of basal progenitor cells.
source: Perpendicular divisions are termed asymmetric divisions because they contribute one daughter cell to the differentiated suprabasal cell layer and do not alter the number of basal progenitor cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about perpendicular cell divisions.

claim: In the embryonic epidermis, asymmetric divisions are used to drive stratification of the skin.
source: In the embryonic epidermis, asymmetric divisions are used to drive stratification of the skin (Lechler and Fuchs, 2005; Smart, 1970; Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In adult backskin most divisions are planar (symmetric).
source: However, in adult backskin most divisions are planar (symmetric) and the utility of regulated spindle orientation has not been explored (Ipponjima et al., 2016; Rompolas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ipponjima et al., 2016 and Rompolas et al., 2016.

claim: In the embryonic mouse epidermis, where proliferation is high, the ratio of perpendicular to planar divisions is approximately 70:30.
source: In the embryonic mouse epidermis, where proliferation is high, the ratio of perpendicular to planar divisions is approximately 70:30 (Lechler and Fuchs, 2005; Smart, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lechler and Fuchs, 2005 and Smart, 1970.

claim: Expression of Cdkn1b in embryonic epidermis resulted in a significant decrease in basal cell proliferation.
source: Quantitation of the percentage of cells expressing the mitotic marker phospho-histone H3 (pHH3) revealed a significant decrease in basal cell proliferation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression of Cdkn1b in embryonic epidermis resulted in a significant reduction in perpendicular divisions, from 70% to 35%.
source: This also resulted in a significant reduction in perpendicular divisions, from 70% to 35%, with a concomitant increase in planar divisions (from 22% to 42%) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Expression of Cdkn1b in embryonic epidermis resulted in an increase in planar divisions from 22% to 42%.
source: This also resulted in a significant reduction in perpendicular divisions, from 70% to 35%, with a concomitant increase in planar divisions (from 22% to 42%) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: The majority of mitotic spindles are planar in adult backskin.
source: Consistent with this observation, we see that the majority of mitotic spindles are planar in adult backskin (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There is regional variability in epidermis from different anatomical areas in both proliferation and spindle orientation.
source: Notably, there is regional variability in epidermis from different anatomical areas in both proliferation and spindle orientation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: The epidermis of the footpad, which is thicker, has both a higher proliferation index and increased numbers of perpendicular divisions.
source: The epidermis of the footpad, which is thicker, has both a higher proliferation index and increased numbers of perpendicular divisions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of Cdkn1b caused a shift to more planar cell divisions in the paw epidermis.
source: Similar to the embryonic epidermis, expression of Cdkn1b caused a shift to more planar cell divisions in the paw epidermis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: TPA treatment resulted in thickening of the epidermis.
source: This resulted in thickening of the epidermis and a 6-fold increase in proliferation rate as measured by BrdU incorporation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TPA treatment resulted in a 6-fold increase in proliferation rate as measured by BrdU incorporation.
source: This resulted in thickening of the epidermis and a 6-fold increase in proliferation rate as measured by BrdU incorporation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TPA treatment increased the percentage of perpendicular divisions from 20% to 40%.
source: Notably, this treatment increased the percentage of perpendicular divisions from 20% to 40% (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: NuMA is essential for spindle orientation in embryonic skin.
source: To directly determine whether regulated spindle orientation was important for epidermal homeostasis we examined the effects of mutating the nuclear mitotic apparatus protein, NuMA, which is essential for spindle orientation in embryonic skin (Williams et al., 2011; Seldin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Williams et al., 2011 and Seldin et al., 2016.

claim: Adult backskin homeostasis is normally maintained by delamination and differentiation rather than by regulated spindle orientation.
source: We did not see significant phenotypes when we disrupted NuMA's spindle orientation function in adult epidermis for short times (data not shown), consistent with findings that adult backskin homeostasis is normally maintained by delamination and differentiation rather than by regulated spindle orientation (Rompolas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rompolas et al., 2016 and inference from experimental data.

claim: Mutations that activate Ras family members can drive squamous cell carcinoma.
source: Mutations that activate Ras family members can drive squamous cell carcinoma and a significant percentage of squamous tumors carry Ras mutations (Daya-Grosjean et al., 1993; Pierceall et al., 1991; South et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A significant percentage of squamous tumors carry Ras mutations.
source: Mutations that activate Ras family members can drive squamous cell carcinoma and a significant percentage of squamous tumors carry Ras mutations (Daya-Grosjean et al., 1993; Pierceall et al., 1991; South et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Expression of KRASG12D had no significant change in division orientation ratios in the backskin.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that expression of KRASG12D (at endogenous levels and only in the epidermis; K5CreER;KRASG12D/+) had distinct effects in backskin and footpad epidermis. While there was no significant change in division orientation ratios in the backskin, active K-Ras resulted in an increase in perpendicular divisions in the footpads (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A-D.

claim: Active K-Ras resulted in an increase in perpendicular divisions in the footpads.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that expression of KRASG12D (at endogenous levels and only in the epidermis; K5CreER;KRASG12D/+) had distinct effects in backskin and footpad epidermis. While there was no significant change in division orientation ratios in the backskin, active K-Ras resulted in an increase in perpendicular divisions in the footpads (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A-D.

claim: Combining a NuMA mutation with the KRASG12D oncogene resulted in a significant shift of divisions from perpendicular to planar.
source: We combined a NuMA mutation that disrupts embryonic spindle orientation with the KRASG12D oncogene (Seldin et al., 2016; Silk et al., 2009). This resulted in a significant shift of divisions from perpendicular to planar, consistent with NuMA being required for spindle orientation in this context (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: NuMA is required for spindle orientation in epidermis expressing active K-Ras.
source: This resulted in a significant shift of divisions from perpendicular to planar, consistent with NuMA being required for spindle orientation in this context (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that NuMA mutation shifts division orientation in KRASG12D background.

claim: Within two weeks of recombination, large overgrowths appeared on the footpads and anogenital regions of the double mutant mice (K5CreER;KRASG12D/+;NuMAMTBDfl/fl).
source: Within two weeks of recombination, large overgrowths appeared on the footpads and anogenital regions of the double mutant mice (K5CreER;KRASG12D/+;NuMAMTBDfl/fl) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Large overgrowths were not found in single KRASG12D or NuMA mutants.
source: These features were not found in single KRASG12D or NuMA mutants, although KRASG12D alone was sufficient for formation of oral tumors similar to those that appeared in the double mutants.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: KRASG12D alone was sufficient for formation of oral tumors.
source: These features were not found in single KRASG12D or NuMA mutants, although KRASG12D alone was sufficient for formation of oral tumors similar to those that appeared in the double mutants.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Most K5CreER;KRASG12D/+;NuMAMTBDfl/fl mice died within 3–4 weeks after recombination.
source: Most mice died within 3–4 weeks after recombination (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The basement membrane remained intact in double mutant paws despite massive tissue overgrowth.
source: Despite this dramatic change in tissue architecture, the basement membrane remained intact and differentiation was normal at early time points.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from histologic analysis.

claim: Differentiation was normal at early time points in double mutant paws.
source: Despite this dramatic change in tissue architecture, the basement membrane remained intact and differentiation was normal at early time points.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from histologic analysis.

claim: The combination of NuMA and KRASG12D mutations is not sufficient for invasion, at least in the short time period assayed.
source: Thus, this combination of mutations is not sufficient for invasion, at least in the short time period we were able to assay.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the basement membrane remained intact.

claim: The massive tissue overgrowth led to lethality, likely due, at least in part, to blockage of the oral cavity.
source: The massive tissue overgrowth led to lethality, likely due, at least in part, to blockage of the oral cavity.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the cause of lethality.

claim: Loss of spindle orientation alone is not detrimental in developing fly wings.
source: Similar to the loss of NuMA function in the adult epidermis, loss of spindle orientation alone is not detrimental in developing fly wings (Nakajima et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nakajima et al., 2013.

claim: In fly wings, tumors form when loss of spindle orientation is combined with additional mutations that inhibited apoptosis.
source: However, tumors form when combined with additional mutations that inhibited apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in reference to fly wing development, implying citation support from the previous sentence.

claim: There was no genetic interaction when mutant p53 was combined with the NuMAΔMTBD deletion.
source: Notably, we saw no genetic interaction when mutant p53 was combined with the NuMAΔMTBD deletion (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Apoptosis is not a major determinant of tissue homeostasis in the epidermis under normal conditions.
source: These data are consistent with the fact that apoptosis is not a major determinant of tissue homeostasis in the epidermis under normal conditions, and demonstrates a specificity for disrupted spindle organization working synergistically with only a subset of oncogenic drivers.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of genetic interaction between p53 and NuMA mutations.

claim: Disrupted spindle organization works synergistically with only a subset of oncogenic drivers.
source: These data are consistent with the fact that apoptosis is not a major determinant of tissue homeostasis in the epidermis under normal conditions, and demonstrates a specificity for disrupted spindle organization working synergistically with only a subset of oncogenic drivers.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects observed with different oncogenic mutations.

claim: Histologic analysis revealed expansion of the stem cell pool in the KRASG12D; NuMAΔMTBD epidermis.
source: Histologic analysis revealed expansion of the stem cell pool in the KRASG12D; NuMAΔMTBD epidermis.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from histologic analysis.

claim: The basement membrane became highly involuted in KRASG12D; NuMAΔMTBD epidermis to accommodate the increase in cell numbers.
source: To accommodate the increase in cell numbers, the basement membrane became highly involuted (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D-G.

claim: There was a 2–4 fold increase in basement membrane length per tissue length in KRASG12D; NuMAΔMTBD epidermis.
source: We quantitated this as basement membrane length per tissue length and found a 2–4 fold increase in this measure, corresponding to a 4–16 fold increase in area (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The 2–4 fold increase in basement membrane length per tissue length corresponds to a 4–16 fold increase in area.
source: We quantitated this as basement membrane length per tissue length and found a 2–4 fold increase in this measure, corresponding to a 4–16 fold increase in area (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a mathematical inference from the linear measurement.

claim: Low-dose TPA treatment caused a subtle yet significant increase in basement membrane length in NuMAΔMTBD mice as compared to control mice.
source: Similarly, we found that low-dose TPA treatment caused a subtle yet significant increase in basement membrane length in NuMAΔMTBD mice as compared to control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Constitutively active KRas expression is not sufficient to drive hyperproliferation in the paw skin.
source: Notably, we found that constitutively active KRas expression is not sufficient to drive hyperproliferation in the paw skin, nor did it do so in combination with a mutation in NuMA (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Constitutively active KRas expression in combination with a mutation in NuMA is not sufficient to drive hyperproliferation in the paw skin.
source: Notably, we found that constitutively active KRas expression is not sufficient to drive hyperproliferation in the paw skin, nor did it do so in combination with a mutation in NuMA (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Active Ras can inhibit differentiation when overexpressed in the epidermis.
source: Previous work has suggested that active Ras can inhibit differentiation when overexpressed in the epidermis (Dajee et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dajee et al., 2002.

claim: In adults, cells commit to differentiation, detach from the basement membrane, and move upward.
source: In adults, cells commit to differentiation, detach from the basement membrane, and move upward.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about adult epidermal cell behavior.

claim: In the pawskin, approximately 10% of basal cells were labeled with H2B-GFP in K10-rtTA;TRE-H2B-GFP mice.
source: In the pawskin, we found that ~10% of basal cells were labeled with H2B-GFP, and this fell to 0.4% two days after removal of doxycycline, consistent with these cells entering differentiation (n>200 cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the K10-rtTA;TRE-H2B-GFP mouse line.

claim: H2B-GFP labeling in basal cells fell to 0.4% two days after removal of doxycycline.
source: In the pawskin, we found that ~10% of basal cells were labeled with H2B-GFP, and this fell to 0.4% two days after removal of doxycycline, consistent with these cells entering differentiation (n>200 cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the K10-rtTA;TRE-H2B-GFP mouse line.

claim: H2B-GFP labeled-basal cells incorporated EdU at a lower rate than surrounding basal cells (28 ± 2.4% for K10-ve basal cells verses 9 ± 3.0% for K10+ve basal cells).
source: Additionally, H2B-GFP labeled-basal cells incorporated EdU at a lower rate than surrounding basal cells (28 ± 2.4% for K10-ve basal cells verses 9 ± 3.0% for K10+ve basal cells, n=3 mice, >400 cells/mouse).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from EdU incorporation assays.

claim: Differentiation was suppressed in KRASG12D expressing cells.
source: Using the K10-rtTA;TRE-H2B-GFP genetic labeling system we found that differentiation was suppressed in KRASG12D expressing cells (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Differentiation suppression by KRASG12D was most dramatic in the paw epidermis, but was also observed in backskin to a lesser extent.
source: This was most dramatic in the paw epidermis, but was also observed in backskin to a lesser extent.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: The relative intensity of β4-integrin was increased in the mutant pawskin.
source: While the mechanism underlying this suppression is not clear, we also found that the relative intensity of β4-integrin was increased in the mutant pawskin, in a similar manner to what was observed when K-Ras was overexpressed in the embryo (Dajee et al., 2002; Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Increased β4-integrin intensity in mutant pawskin is similar to what was observed when K-Ras was overexpressed in the embryo.
source: While the mechanism underlying this suppression is not clear, we also found that the relative intensity of β4-integrin was increased in the mutant pawskin, in a similar manner to what was observed when K-Ras was overexpressed in the embryo (Dajee et al., 2002; Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dajee et al., 2002 and experimental data.

claim: Robust adhesion and signaling through integrins is known to promote progenitor cell fate.
source: Robust adhesion and signaling through integrins is known to promote progenitor cell fate, and thus may contribute to the changes in differentiation that we observed.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about integrin signaling.

claim: Robust adhesion and signaling through integrins may contribute to the changes in differentiation observed in KRASG12D expressing cells.
source: Robust adhesion and signaling through integrins is known to promote progenitor cell fate, and thus may contribute to the changes in differentiation that we observed.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of differentiation suppression.

claim: The epidermis can respond to changes in homeostasis by altering mitotic spindle orientation.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that the epidermis can respond to changes in homeostasis by altering mitotic spindle orientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Increasing perpendicular (asymmetric) divisions in response to either increased proliferation or decreased differentiation allows homeostasis to be reset without dramatically affecting tissue architecture.
source: Increasing perpendicular (asymmetric) divisions in response to either increased proliferation or decreased differentiation allows homeostasis to be reset without dramatically affecting tissue architecture.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Regulation of spindle orientation is essential to prevent tissue overgrowth in an oncogenic background.
source: Our genetic analysis clearly shows that this is essential to prevent tissue overgrowth in an oncogenic background.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments with KRASG12D and NuMA mutations.

claim: The epidermis responded differently to the same oncogenic insult at different anatomic sites.
source: In addition, we found that the epidermis responded differently to the same oncogenic insult at different anatomic sites.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: The different responses to oncogenic insult at different anatomic sites likely reflects the differences in proliferation, differentiation, and rates of asymmetric cell division rates in different regions of the epidermis.
source: This likely reflects the differences in proliferation, differentiation, and rates of asymmetric cell division rates in different regions of the epidermis and suggests that distinct 'second hits' may be needed to collaborate with oncogenes in tissues with different mechanisms of achieving homeostasis.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the cause of regional differences.

claim: Distinct 'second hits' may be needed to collaborate with oncogenes in tissues with different mechanisms of achieving homeostasis.
source: This likely reflects the differences in proliferation, differentiation, and rates of asymmetric cell division rates in different regions of the epidermis and suggests that distinct 'second hits' may be needed to collaborate with oncogenes in tissues with different mechanisms of achieving homeostasis.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about oncogenic collaboration.

claim: Both regulated spindle orientation and delamination/differentiation can be used to buffer basal cell number.
source: Our data are consistent with the idea that both regulated spindle orientation and delamination/differentiation can be used to buffer basal cell number.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Disruption of either regulated spindle orientation or delamination/differentiation alone was insufficient to induce homeostatic defects due to compensation by the other.
source: Disruption of either one was insufficient to induce homeostatic defects due to compensation by the other.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Blockade of both homeostatic buffers (regulated spindle orientation and delamination/differentiation) resulted in tissue overgrowth and progenitor cell expansion.
source: However, blockade of both homeostatic buffers resulted in tissue overgrowth and progenitor cell expansion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with double mutants.

claim: Squamous cell carcinomas have been reported to have increased rates of perpendicular divisions as compared to normal epidermis.
source: Notably, squamous cell carcinomas have been reported to have increased rates of perpendicular divisions as compared to normal epidermis (Beck et al., 2011; Siegle et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beck et al., 2011 and Siegle et al., 2014.

claim: Regulated spindle orientation may be protective against tumor development in squamous cell carcinomas.
source: It will be important to see whether regulated spindle orientation is protective against tumor development in these contexts.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the potential role of spindle orientation in tumor protection.

claim: Spindle angles were measured as the angle formed by a line drawn through the two spindle poles and a second line across the underlying basement membrane.
source: Spindle angles were measured in Fiji and defined by the angle formed by a line drawn through the two spindle poles of late metaphase or anaphase spindles and a second line across the underlying basement membrane (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: When spindle poles were not in the same plane, three dimensional reconstructions were generated and spindle angles were measured in rotated images.
source: When spindle poles were not in the same plane, three dimensional reconstructions were generated and spindle angles were measured in rotated images.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.
